cor-est-estimable-space.title: The estimable space
cor-est-estimable-space.html:
The set of 𝛌λ for which 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable is the subspace C(X⊤) of dimension r=rank(X). In particular:

  1. every expected response 𝛃x(i)⊤β, and hence the whole mean vector 𝛃Xβ, is estimable;

  2. every entry of 𝛃X⊤Xβ is estimable;

  3. at most r estimable functions can be linearly independent, and a set of r linearly independent ones determines all the others as linear combinations;

  4. if r=p, every linear function of 𝛃β is estimable.

def-est-coding.title: Coding of a factor
def-est-coding.html: A coding of a factor with g levels is a nonsingular g×g matrix K. The coded model matrix is ZK, and the model is 𝛄E(Y)=ZKγ. When the first column of K is 1g, so that K=[1g,C], the coded matrix is [1n,ZC]: an intercept and the g−1 columns ZC. The g×(g−1) matrix C is then called the coding matrix of the factor.

def-est-contrast.title: Contrast
def-est-contrast.html: In a factor model, a contrast in the effects of a factor is a linear function ∑kckαk whose coefficients satisfy ∑kck=0, not all zero. In the one-way model it equals ∑kckμk, and we call either form a contrast in the level means. Two contrasts are orthogonal (for the given design) if ∑kckdk/nk=0.

def-est-estimable.title: Estimable function
def-est-estimable.html: A linear function 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β, 𝛌λ∈Rp, is estimable if there is a vector a∈Rn such that 𝛌𝛃𝛃E(a⊤Y)=λ⊤βfor every β∈Rp. A vector 𝛃Λ⊤β of linear functions, with Λ a p×q matrix, is estimable if each of its q components is. Equivalently, there is an n×q matrix A with 𝛃E(A⊤Y)=Λ⊤β for all 𝛃β.

def-est-identifiable.title: Identifiability
def-est-identifiable.html: In the linear model 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, 𝛃β∈Rp, the parameter 𝛃β is identifiable if 𝛃𝛃Xβ1=Xβ2 implies 𝛃𝛃β1=β2. A function g defined on Rp, with values in any set, is identifiable if 𝛃𝛃Xβ1=Xβ2 implies 𝛃𝛃g(β1)=g(β2).

eq-est-H.html: HG=GX⊤X.

eq-est-additive.html: E(y)=μ+αi+βjfor an observation in cell (i,j),

eq-est-contrast-var.html: ψ^=∑kcky¯k,Var(ψ^)=σ2∑kck2nk.

eq-est-contrast-vector.html: uc=ZD−1c,

eq-est-fibre.html: 𝛃𝛃{b∈Rp:Xb=Xβ}=β+N(X),

eq-est-indicator-facts.html: Z1g=1n,Z⊤Z=D=diag(n1,…,ng),Z⊤y=(y1⋅,…,yg⋅)⊤,

eq-est-interaction.html: E(y)=μ+αi+βj+γijfor an observation in cell (i,j),

eq-est-ls-as-linear.html: 𝛌𝛃𝛃λ⊤β^=a⊤Xβ^=a⊤My=(Ma)⊤y,

eq-est-parallel.html: E(y)=μk+θxfor an observation at level k,

eq-est-reparameterization-matrix.html: Z=XU⊤(UU⊤)−1.

eq-est-separate.html: E(y)=μk+θkx,

eq-est-side-solution.html: 𝛃β^T=(X⊤X+T⊤T)−1X⊤y,

exm-est-adjusted.title: Education and television news, adjusted for age
exm-est-adjusted.title_html: Education and television news, adjusted for age
exm-est-adjusted.html:
In the ANES data, respondents report how many times per week they watch television news. Coding education with seven levels and “high-school graduate” as the reference, respondents with some high school but no diploma watch 1.005 times a week more than high-school graduates. They are also older, with mean ages 59.8 and 48.2, and news watching rises with age. Adding age to the model, the within-level slope is 0.0674 times per week per year of age, and the adjusted difference shrinks to 0.224. More than three quarters of the raw difference is an age difference, and @prp-est-adjusted accounts for it exactly. Whether the adjusted figure is the “effect of education” is a different question. Here age plausibly influences both schooling (older cohorts had less of it) and viewing habits, which argues for adjusting, but Chapter 25 shows that adjustment is not always appropriate.

Allowing separate age slopes for three education groups (codes 1–3, high school or less, 313 respondents; codes 4–5, 277; and the two highest levels, codes 6–7, 354) gives slopes 0.0686, 0.0729 and 0.0597, close to the common slope 0.0672 of the parallel lines model with the same three groups. The residual sum of squares falls only from 5623.6 to 5616.7 for the two extra parameters. Figure 8.6.1 shows the three fitted lines with binned means. The lines are nearly parallel, and the highest education group starts higher and rises a little more slowly.

exm-est-apc.title: Age, period and cohort
exm-est-apc.html:
A survey is fielded every five years from 2000 to 2020, and its respondents are grouped in eleven five-year age bands from 20 to 70. For each of the 55 combinations we have one average response. A demographer wants to separate three linear trends: in age (people change as they grow older), in period (everyone changes with the times), and in birth cohort (generations differ). With age, period and cohort centred at 45, 2010 and 1965, the model is E(y)=β0+βAage+βPperiod+βCcohort. But cohort is period minus age, for every respondent. The four columns satisfy age−period+cohort=0, so v=(0,1,−1,1)⊤ spans N(X) and rank(X)=3. By @prp-est-coordinate, none of the three slopes is identifiable.

The listing fits the model three times, each time dropping one of the three columns. All three fits have residual sum of squares 157.00, because they have the same column space. They tell three different stories:

Fit age slope period slope cohort slope
no cohort term 0.102 0.092 0.000
no period term 0.194 0.000 0.092
no age term 0.000 0.194 -0.102

One analyst reports a steady ageing effect and no generational change. Another reports a strong ageing effect and a positive cohort trend. A third reports no ageing at all, a strong secular trend, and younger generations scoring lower. The data were in fact simulated with slopes 0.30, −0.10 and 0.20. That vector lies on the parallel line 𝛃β+tv of equally valid truths, and the data cannot prefer it. Only the identifiable combinations are recovered: the fitted 0.194 and 0.092 estimate the true 0.20 and 0.10.

What the three fits share are the linear functions orthogonal to v=(0,1,−1,1)⊤: βA+βP=0.194,βP+βC=0.092,βA−βC=0.102, in every row of the table, and β0. Any statement about the separate trends requires information from outside these data, for instance a constraint justified by subject knowledge, and the conclusions then rest on that constraint (@exr-est-apc-factors). Figure 8.1.1 shows how each fit divides the same fitted surface among the three terms.

exm-est-connected.title: Two islands
exm-est-connected.html: Take a=4, b=5 and seven occupied cells: (1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(2,3) and (3,4),(4,4),(4,5) (levels numbered from 1). The design graph has two components: rows 1–2 with columns 1–3, and rows 3–4 with columns 4–5. By @thm-est-connected, rank(X)=4+5−2=7, one less than a+b−1=8. The difference α1−α2 is estimable, since rows 1 and 2 are linked through column 2, but α1−α3 is not. The two islands could sit at any vertical offset from each other without changing any fitted value. Occupying a single further cell, (3,3), joins the islands. The rank rises to 8, and α1−α3 becomes estimable. The listing checks each statement with the rank test @thm-est-characterization(h). The script also checks the rank formula on 200 random designs.

exm-est-empty-cells.title: Empty cells in a survey
exm-est-empty-cells.html: Cross-classify the 944 ANES respondents of @exm-est-party-coding by party identification (seven levels) and education (seven levels, labelled in the statsmodels documentation from “grades 1–8” to “PhD”). Two of the 49 cells are empty: no pure independent and no weak Republican in the sample has only an elementary-school education. Other cells are thin: only 3 pure independents report some high school. The overparameterized interaction model has p=64 columns and rank 47, the number of occupied cells, as @prp-est-interaction(a) says. The interaction contrast comparing strong Democrats with pure independents across “some high school” and “high-school graduate” involves four occupied cells and is estimable. It rests on only 3 respondents in one cell, so it is imprecise, but estimable. The same comparison across “grades 1–8” and “high-school graduate” involves an empty cell and is not estimable. No amount of computation will produce it, and software that prints a number for it is printing an artefact of its side condition. The additive model, with rank 7+7−1=13, treats both comparisons as zero by assumption.

exm-est-five-conditions.title: Five side conditions, one fit
exm-est-five-conditions.html:
Eighteen simulated observations fall into four groups of sizes 5,3,6,4, with group means 11.111, 15.204, 10.558 and 13.624. In the model E(ykj)=μ+αk, p−r=1, so a side condition is a single nonestimable restriction. The listing solves @eq-est-side-solution for five of them and computes the minimum-norm solution.

Side condition μ^ α^1 α^2 α^3 α^4
α1=0 11.111 0.000 4.093 -0.553 2.513
α4=0 13.624 -2.513 1.580 -3.066 0.000
∑kαk=0 12.624 -1.513 2.580 -2.066 1.000
∑knkαk=0 12.167 -1.056 3.037 -1.609 1.457
μ=0 0.000 11.111 15.204 10.558 13.624
minimum norm (μ=∑kαk) 10.100 1.012 5.105 0.459 3.525

Every row solves the normal equations. In every row μ^+α^k is the kth group mean, and α^1−α^2 is the same. The value of μ^ is, in turn, the first group mean, the last group mean, the average of the four group means (12.624), the overall mean y¯=12.167, zero, and an uninterpretable 10.100.

Compare a restriction that is estimable, α1=α2. It is not a side condition. Imposing it (by solving the Lagrange system for least squares under a linear restriction) forces the first two group means to be equal. The residual sum of squares rises from 14.665 to 46.078. The fit has changed, which is what testing the hypothesis α1=α2 in Chapter 11 measures.

exm-est-fixed-ratio.title: A fertilizer trial with a fixed ratio
exm-est-fixed-ratio.title_html: A fertilizer trial with a fixed ratio
exm-est-fixed-ratio.html:
Ten plots receive nitrogen at 0,20,40,60,80 kg/ha (two plots each), and phosphorus is always applied at half the nitrogen rate, as in a commercial blend. The model E(y)=β0+β1N+β2P is natural agronomically, but in this design xP=12xN, so v=(0,1,−2)⊤ spans N(X) and rank(X)=2. A linear function is estimable iff its coefficient vector satisfies λ1−2λ2=0. So:

  • β0, the mean yield without fertilizer, is estimable. Plots with N=P=0 were observed.
  • The mean yield at (N,P)=(40,20) is estimable, since 40−2⋅20=0, and so is the mean at any dose of the blend, observed or not, such as (50,25).
  • The mean yield at (40,0), nitrogen alone, is not estimable, since 40−0≠0.
  • Neither β1 nor β2 is estimable, but β1+12β2, the gain per kilogram of nitrogen when it comes with its phosphorus, is.

The listing computes three least squares solutions: the minimum-norm one, the one that omits P, and the one that omits N. They give intercepts 2.9579, 2.9579 and 2.9579, all equal as they must be. The pairs of slopes (0.0296,0.0148), (0.0370,0.0000) and (0.0000,0.0740) all disagree. At the blend dose (40,20) all three predict 4.439 t/ha. At the nitrogen-only dose (40,0) they predict 4.143, 4.439 and 2.958. The third value is just β^0, because that solution puts the whole fertilizer effect on phosphorus. Each of these is a legitimate least squares answer, and none of them estimates anything.

The two kinds of prediction differ in kind, not in degree. Nothing in this experiment says what nitrogen does without phosphorus. A larger experiment of the same design would not help. What is needed is at least one plot off the line P=N/2 (@exr-est-new-row).

exm-est-near-estimable.title: Estimable in principle, not in practice
exm-est-near-estimable.title_html: Estimable in principle, not in practice
exm-est-near-estimable.html:
Take twelve equally spaced values ti on [−1,1] and the model matrix with columns 1, t and t+δw, where wi=cos⁡(πti) and δ is a small perturbation. At δ=0 the last two columns coincide. Then β1+β2 is estimable and β1 is not. For δ>0 the matrix has full rank, so everything is estimable. But Figure 8.3.1 shows how the variance of β^1 grows as δ→0: in proportion to 1/δ2 (the fitted slope on the log–log scale is −2.00). At δ=10−4, the smallest singular value of X is 1.8×10−4, and Var(β^1)=1.56×107σ2, while Var(β^1+β^2)=0.212σ2 is unaffected. The function that is estimable at δ=0 stays well estimated, and the one that is not becomes useless long before it becomes nonestimable.

The listing adds a warning about computation. At δ=10−8, the SVD of X still sees three nonzero singular values, so β1 is (barely) estimable. But the matrix X⊤X has eigenvalues equal to the squared singular values. Its smallest eigenvalue is about 3×10−16, below any sensible tolerance, and pinv(X.T @ X) silently treats X⊤X as having rank 2. It then reports 0.0529 as the “variance” of β^1, which is the Moore–Penrose quadratic form of a nonestimable function. The true variance, computed from the SVD of X itself, is more than 1016 times larger. Forming X⊤X squares the condition number, as Section 6.10 showed, and here that turns a nearly nonestimable function into a numerically nonestimable one.

exm-est-oneway-checks.title: Checking estimability in a one-way layout
exm-est-oneway-checks.title_html: Checking estimability in a one-way layout
exm-est-oneway-checks.html:
Eighteen observations fall into four groups of sizes 4,6,3,5, with X=[1,z1,z2,z3,z4] and 𝛃β=(μ,α1,…,α4)⊤, so rank(X)=4 and N(X) is spanned by (1,−1,−1,−1,−1)⊤. By condition (c), 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable iff λ0=λ1+λ2+λ3+λ4. The listing tests five vectors in two ways: condition (c) through the SVD of X, and condition (e) with three generalized inverses (Moore–Penrose, the one that deletes the intercept row and column, and a non-symmetric one built as in @prp-mat-ginverse-props(e)). The two tests always agree, and condition (e) holds for all three inverses or for none, as (f) requires.

𝛌𝛃λ⊤β estimable 𝛌𝛌λ⊤Gλ: Moore–Penrose drop intercept non-symmetric
μ+α1 yes 0.250 0.250 0.250
α1−α2 yes 0.417 0.417 0.417
α1+α2−2α3 yes 1.750 1.750 1.750
α1 no 0.188 0.250 0.630
α1+α2+α3+α4 no 0.038 0.950 2.767

For the estimable rows the quadratic form is the same for all three and matches the direct computation: Var(y¯1−y¯2)=σ2(14+16), for instance. For α1 the “variances” disagree. With the drop-intercept inverse, the solution is 𝛃β^G=(0,y¯1,…,y¯4)⊤, so the reported “α^1” is y¯1, which estimates μ+α1. Its reported variance 0.250σ2 is the variance of y¯1, which is correct, but y¯1 estimates μ+α1, not α1.

exm-est-party-coding.title: Party identification and ideology
exm-est-party-coding.html:
An extract of the 1996 American National Election Study, distributed with statsmodels as a public-domain data set, contains 944 respondents who placed themselves on a seven-point scale from extremely liberal (1) to extremely conservative (7). It also records their party identification in seven levels from strong Democrat to strong Republican. The level means and sizes are

party identification strong Dem weak Dem ind. Dem independent ind. Rep weak Rep strong Rep
nk 200 180 108 37 94 150 175
y¯k 3.335 3.617 3.685 4.054 4.957 5.033 5.691

Here are the coefficients of four codings of the same factor (γ1,…,γ6 refer to the columns of C in the order defined above; for the two deviation codings they belong to the first six levels):

coding γ^0 γ^1 γ^2 γ^3 γ^4 γ^5 γ^6
reference (strong Dem) 3.335 0.282 0.350 0.719 1.622 1.698 2.356
sum to zero 4.339 -1.004 -0.722 -0.654 -0.285 0.618 0.694
weighted effect 4.325 -0.990 -0.709 -0.640 -0.271 0.632 0.708
successive differences 4.339 0.282 0.069 0.369 0.903 0.076 0.658

Each row is 𝛍K−1μ^ for its own K, as @prp-est-coding(b) says, and all four have residual sum of squares 1178.3. The intercepts are the reference mean 3.335, the unweighted mean of the seven means 4.339, the overall mean y¯=4.325 and again 4.339. Figure 8.5.1 shows the three reference points. The successive differences show that the largest step in ideology, 0.903, falls between pure independents and independents leaning Republican, and the step between weak and strong Republicans is 0.658. The reference coding cannot show this directly. The two deviation codings nearly agree here because the groups are of similar size, apart from the small group of pure independents.

exm-est-party-trend.title: Trend in ideology across party identification
exm-est-party-trend.title_html: Trend in ideology across party identification
exm-est-party-trend.html:
Return to the seven party-identification groups of @exm-est-party-coding. The between-group sum of squares is 772.87. The classical linear contrast has estimate ψ^=∑k(k−4)y¯k=11.175, variance 0.1652σ2 by @eq-est-contrast-var, and sum of squares 755.85, which is 97.8 percent of the between-group sum of squares. The quadratic and cubic contrasts have sums of squares 10.15 and 2.58. Ideology rises almost linearly across the seven-point party scale, with some upward curvature (Figure 8.7.1).

The group sizes range from 37 to 200, so the six classical contrasts are not orthogonal for this design. Their sums of squares add to 784.02, which exceeds the between-group total. Part of the variation is counted twice. The weighted orthogonal polynomial contrasts decompose the total exactly: 746.57 for the linear trend and 26.30 for the five higher-degree contrasts together.

exr-est-ancova-identifiable.title: B1
exr-est-ancova-identifiable.html: Let Z=[z1,…,zg] be the indicator matrix of a factor and x a numeric covariate, and consider X=[1,Z,x]. Show that the slope of x is identifiable iff x∉C(Z), that is, iff x is not constant within every level. Show that no intercept-type parameter β0 or αk is identifiable.

exr-est-any-variance.title: C1
exr-est-any-variance.html: Let 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β be nonestimable. Show that as G ranges over all generalized inverses of X⊤X, the number 𝛌𝛌λ⊤Gλ takes every real value, including negative ones. So the “variance” that software attaches to a nonestimable function can be anything at all.

exr-est-apc-basis.title: A1
exr-est-apc-basis.html: In @exm-est-apc, show directly that β0, βA+βP and βP+βC are identifiable, that every identifiable linear function is a combination of these three, and that βA−βC is one of them. Is βA+βC identifiable?

exr-est-apc-factors.title: C1
exr-est-apc-factors.html: Replace the three linear terms of @exm-est-apc by three factors: an indicator for each age band, each period and each cohort (with an intercept). Show that the null space of the resulting model matrix has dimension 3 plus exactly one extra dimension. Identify the extra null vector: it assigns the linear sequences a−a¯, −(t−t¯) and c−c¯ to the age, period and cohort effects. Deduce that every second difference of age effects, such as αa+1−2αa+αa−1, is identifiable, while no linear trend in any single one of the three factors is.

exr-est-bad-side.title: C2
exr-est-bad-side.html: Suppose rank(T)=p−r but C(T⊤)∩C(X⊤)≠{0}. Show that for some y the restricted normal equations of @thm-est-side-conditions(a) have no solution, and that whenever they have one they have infinitely many.

exr-est-broken.title: B2
exr-est-broken.html: Write the broken-line model E(y)=β0+β1x+β2(x−c)+ in matrix form and prove the identifiability condition stated in the text. Show that the continuous broken line is the same as the model with two separate lines, one on each side of c, constrained to meet at c, and count parameters to explain the difference of one.

exr-est-coding-side.title: C1
exr-est-coding-side.html: Show that fitting the reference-coded model is the same as solving the normal equations of the overparameterized one-way model under the side condition α1=0, with γ0=μ and γj=αj+1. State and prove the corresponding facts for the sum-to-zero and weighted effect codings.

exr-est-counts.title: B3
exr-est-counts.html: On each of m days a warehouse runs N1i machines of type 1 and N2i of type 2, and meters its total energy use Vi. Suppose each running machine of type k uses an amount of energy with mean θk and variance τk2, independently of the other machines and the same on every day. Show that E(Vi)=θ1N1i+θ2N2i, a linear model without intercept, and that (θ1,θ2) is identifiable iff the vectors (N1i) and (N2i) are not proportional. Find Cov(V); why is it not a multiple of I? Why is it essential that θk does not vary by day?

exr-est-cov-pd.title: B2
exr-est-cov-pd.html: Let 𝛃Λ⊤β be estimable with Λ of full column rank q, and suppose Cov(Y)=σ2I with σ2>0. Show that 𝛃Cov(Λ⊤β^)=σ2Λ⊤GΛ is positive definite, whichever generalized inverse is used. Hint: write Λ=X⊤P and show MP has full column rank.

exr-est-cumulative.title: B2
exr-est-cumulative.html: For an ordered factor with g levels, let the coded columns be the indicators of {level≥k}, k=2,…,g, together with an intercept. Show that K is lower triangular with ones on and below the diagonal, that K−1 is the first-difference matrix, and hence that the coefficients are μ1 and μk−μk−1.

exr-est-design-planning.title: B3
exr-est-design-planning.html: A study will compare three treatments, A, B and C, in the additive model E(y)=μ+τtrt+δsite. Two sites are available, and each site can host two of the three treatments. Which allocations make every difference τs−τt estimable? Show that putting {A,B} at both sites leaves τA−τC nonestimable, while {A,B} at one site and {B,C} at the other makes all three differences estimable.

exr-est-disconnected.title: C1
exr-est-disconnected.html: In the additive model, let the design graph have components C1,…,Cc. Show that λ0μ+∑iλiαi+∑jκjβj is estimable iff λ0=∑jκj and, for every component C, ∑i∈Cλi=∑j∈Cκj. Deduce @thm-est-connected(b).

exr-est-drop-columns.title: B1
exr-est-drop-columns.html: Let X=[X1,X2], where X1 has full column rank and C(X1)=C(X). Show that the least squares fit using X1 alone, padded with zeros for the coefficients of X2, is the solution of the side condition T=[0,I]. Check the conditions of @thm-est-side-conditions directly.

exr-est-fixed-ratio-list.title: A1
exr-est-fixed-ratio-list.html: In @exm-est-fixed-ratio, decide which of the following are estimable: β1−2β2; 2β1+β2; the mean yield at (N,P)=(100,50); the mean yield at (0,10); the difference between the mean yields at (60,30) and (20,10). For the estimable ones give a vector a with 𝛌X⊤a=λ.

exr-est-general-interaction.title: B3
exr-est-general-interaction.html: In the interaction model, suppose all cells are occupied except (1,1). Show that the (a−1)(b−1) contrasts γij−γi1−γ1j+γ11 are no longer estimable, but that γij−γi2−γ1j+γ12 is estimable for i≥2, j≥3. How many linearly independent estimable interaction contrasts remain?

exr-est-helmert-balance.title: A2
exr-est-helmert-balance.html: Show that the Helmert contrasts h2,…,hg are orthogonal for the design iff n1=n2=⋯=ng−1, whatever ng is. Hint: compute ∑khjkhlk/nk for j<l.

exr-est-identifiable-cosets.title: B2
exr-est-identifiable-cosets.html: Let P be the orthogonal projection onto C(X⊤). Show that g is identifiable iff 𝛃𝛃g(β)=g(Pβ) for every 𝛃β. Deduce that the identifiable functions are exactly the functions of 𝛃Pβ, and that 𝛃Pβ is the unique coefficient vector in C(X⊤) representing the mean 𝛃Xβ.

exr-est-lagrange.title: B3
exr-est-lagrange.html: Let T satisfy the conditions of @thm-est-side-conditions and have full row rank p−r. Show that the bordered matrix (X⊤XT⊤T0) is nonsingular, that the solution of the bordered system with right-hand side (X⊤y,0) has first block 𝛃β^T and second block 0, and interpret the zero Lagrange multiplier. Relate this to @exr-proj-side-conditions.

exr-est-linear-trend.title: C1
exr-est-linear-trend.html: Let x be the n-vector giving each observation’s score sk. Show that the sum of squares of the weighted linear contrast c1=Dp1 equals the regression sum of squares ‖(M1−n−111⊤)y‖2 of the simple regression of y on x with intercept, where M1 projects onto C([1,x]). Conclude that the remaining weighted contrasts together measure the lack of fit of the straight line to the level means.

exr-est-ls-unique-in-C.title: B1
exr-est-ls-unique-in-C.html: Let 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β be estimable and let a∗=Ma as in @eq-est-ls-as-linear. Show that a∗ does not depend on which solution a of 𝛌X⊤a=λ is used, that 𝛌a∗=XGλ for any generalized inverse G of X⊤X, and that 𝛌𝛌‖a∗‖2=λ⊤Gλ.

exr-est-max-contrast.title: B1
exr-est-max-contrast.html: Show that for every contrast c, SS(c)≤∑knk(y¯k−y¯)2, with equality when ck=nk(y¯k−y¯). This fact is the basis of Scheffé’s method in Chapter 13 (@thm-mc-scheffe).

exr-est-mean-at-x0.title: B1
exr-est-mean-at-x0.html: In the separate lines model, show that the mean at level k and covariate value x0, μk+θkx0, is estimable iff either x varies within level k, or x0 equals the common value of x on level k. Interpret this as a statement about extrapolation.

exr-est-min-norm-scale.title: C1
exr-est-min-norm-scale.html: Replace X by XD for a nonsingular diagonal D (a change of units). Show that the minimum-norm solution for XD, converted back to the original units, is the solution for the side condition V0⊤D−2b=0, which differs in general from V0⊤b=0. Conclude that the minimum-norm convention depends on the units of measurement, while no estimable function does.

exr-est-new-row.title: B3
exr-est-new-row.html: A design with model matrix X of rank r<p is augmented by one more observation at a point x0. Show that the rank increases iff x0∉C(X⊤). Show that, in the age–period–cohort design, no additional observation can make the slopes identifiable, and explain why in words.

exr-est-nonlinear-unbiased.title: C1
exr-est-nonlinear-unbiased.html: Suppose the distribution of 𝛆ε does not depend on 𝛃β. Show that if some statistic f(Y), linear or not, satisfies 𝛃Ef(Y)=g(β) for every 𝛃β, then g is identifiable. Conclude that no statistic whatever is unbiased for a nonestimable linear function.

exr-est-oneway-list.title: A1
exr-est-oneway-list.html: In @exm-est-oneway-checks, decide which of the following are estimable, using condition (c): 2μ+α1+α2; α1+α2−α3−α4; μ; 4μ+α1+α2+α3+α4. For each estimable one give its least squares estimator in terms of the group means and its variance.

exr-est-poly4.title: A1
exr-est-poly4.html: Find the linear, quadratic and cubic orthogonal polynomial contrasts for g=4 equally spaced levels, scaled to integers. Check that they are mutually orthogonal and that the quadratic contrast vanishes when μk=a+bk.

exr-est-projection-split.title: C2
exr-est-projection-split.html: Let P be the orthogonal projection onto C(X⊤). Show that the minimum-norm least squares solution 𝛃β^+ satisfies 𝛃𝛃E(β^+)=Pβ, and that for any 𝛌λ, 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β^+ is the least squares estimator of the estimable function 𝛌𝛃(Pλ)⊤β. Interpret 𝛌Pλ as the estimable function “closest” to 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β.

exr-est-separate-rank.title: A2
exr-est-separate-rank.html: A factor has three levels, and the covariate x is constant on level 2 but varies on levels 1 and 3. Find the rank of the separate lines model matrix [Z,Z∘x], and say which of μ1,μ2,μ3,θ1,θ2,θ3 are identifiable.

exr-est-shares.title: A2
exr-est-shares.html: A household’s spending is split into food, housing and other, with shares s1+s2+s3=1. A regression of savings on an intercept and all three shares is proposed. Find N(X) (assuming the shares vary enough that there is no other relation among the columns), decide which coefficients are identifiable, and describe two standard ways to make the model identifiable.

exr-est-single-dummy.title: B1
exr-est-single-dummy.html:
Let X have full column rank, let ei be the ith coordinate vector with ei∉C(X), and fit [X,ei] with coefficients 𝛃(β,δ). Write e^i and hii for the residual and the leverage (@def-proj-leverage) of observation i in the fit of X alone.

  1. Use @thm-proj-fwl, with ei as the regressor of interest and X as the one partialled out, to show that δ^=e^i/(1−hii), and explain why hii<1.

  2. Show that the enlarged fit reproduces yi exactly, and that its 𝛃β^ is the estimate 𝛃β^(i) without observation i.

  3. Deduce the deletion identity 𝛃yi−x(i)⊤β^(i)=e^i/(1−hii): the error in predicting yi from the other observations is the ordinary residual inflated by 1/(1−hii).

exr-est-trap.title: A2
exr-est-trap.html: For a factor with three levels, write down the null space of [1,z1,z2,z3]. Show that adding a second factor’s full set of indicators, [1,ZA,ZB], creates a null space of dimension at least two, and give two independent null vectors.

exr-est-two-by-two.title: A1
exr-est-two-by-two.html: In the additive model with a=b=2, suppose cells (1,1), (2,1) and (2,2) are occupied and (1,2) is empty. Find the rank of X and a basis of N(X). Show that μ+α1+β2, the mean of the empty cell, is estimable by writing it as a combination of the means of occupied cells.

exr-est-two-points.title: A2
exr-est-two-points.html: In simple linear regression E(yi)=β0+β1xi, show that β1 is estimable iff the xi are not all equal. If all xi=c, which linear functions are estimable, and what is their least squares estimator?

exr-est-two-sample.title: A1
exr-est-two-sample.html: In the model E(yi)=β0+β1di, with n0 observations in group 0 (level 1) and n1 in group 1 (level 2), write down the coding matrix K with 𝛍𝛃μ=Kβ. Use @prp-est-coding(b), not an inverse of X⊤X, to find 𝛃β^. Then show that Var(β^1)=σ2(1/n0+1/n1) and that β^1/se(β^1) is the pooled two-sample t statistic, where s2=SSE/(n−2) replaces σ2.

exr-est-two-way-reparameterization.title: B2
exr-est-two-way-reparameterization.html: For the additive model E(yij)=μ+αi+βj with i=1,2, j=1,2,3 and one observation per cell, take U with rows giving μ+α1+β1, α2−α1, β2−β1 and β3−β1. Compute Z from @eq-est-reparameterization-matrix, and check that it is the reference-coded model matrix.

exr-est-unbalanced-rows.title: B2
exr-est-unbalanced-rows.html: In the additive two-way model with nij observations in cell (i,j), show that E(y¯i⋅⋅)=μ+αi+∑jnijβj/ni⋅. Deduce that ∑iciy¯i⋅⋅ is unbiased for every row contrast and every 𝛃β iff the proportions nij/ni⋅ do not depend on i, that is, iff the cell counts are proportional, nij=ni⋅n⋅j/n.

exr-est-valid-sides.title: A1
exr-est-valid-sides.html: In the one-way model with four groups and 𝛃β=(μ,α1,…,α4)⊤, decide which of the following are side conditions in the sense of @thm-est-side-conditions: (i) α2=0; (ii) μ=α3; (iii) α1−α2=0; (iv) α1=0 together with α2=0; (v) 2μ+α1+α2=0.

exr-est-vector-estimable.title: B2
exr-est-vector-estimable.html: Show that 𝛃Λ⊤β is estimable iff Λ⊤b1=Λ⊤b2 whenever Xb1=Xb2, and that in that case 𝛃Λ⊤β^=P⊤My for any P with X⊤P=Λ. Show also that P⊤M does not depend on the choice of P.

exr-est-what-is-reported.title: B1
exr-est-what-is-reported.html: In @exm-est-oneway-checks, compute HG for the drop-intercept generalized inverse, and identify the estimable function 𝛌𝛃λ⊤HGβ that the software is really estimating when it reports “α^k”. Do the same for the generalized inverse that deletes the row and column of α4.

lem-est-affine-unbiased.html: The statistic a0+a⊤Y is unbiased for 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β, for every 𝛃β, iff a0=0 and 𝛌X⊤a=λ.

prp-est-H.title: The matrix \G\X\T\X
prp-est-H.title_html: The matrix GX⊤X
prp-est-H.html:
For any generalized inverse G of X⊤X, with HG as in @eq-est-H:

  1. HG is idempotent, N(HG)=N(X), rank(HG)=r, and the rows of HG span C(X⊤);

  2. 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable iff 𝛌𝛌λ⊤HG=λ⊤;

  3. the solution 𝛃β^G=GX⊤Y has 𝛃𝛃E(β^G)=HGβ. So for every 𝛌λ, 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β^G is unbiased for the estimable function 𝛌𝛃λ⊤HGβ, which equals 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β iff 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable;

  4. for the Moore–Penrose inverse G=(X⊤X)+, HG is the orthogonal projection onto C(X⊤).

prp-est-adjusted.title: Adjusted differences
prp-est-adjusted.html: In the parallel lines model @eq-est-parallel with x∉C(Z), let y¯k and x¯k be the level means. Then θ^=∑k∑i∈k(xi−x¯k)(yi−y¯k)∑k∑i∈k(xi−x¯k)2,μ^k−μ^l=(y¯k−y¯l)−θ^(x¯k−x¯l).

prp-est-coding.title: What a coding estimates
prp-est-coding.html:
Let K be a coding and 𝛍μ^=D−1Z⊤y the vector of level means. Then:

  1. C(ZK)=C(Z), so every coding has the same fitted values, residuals and residual sum of squares;

  2. the coefficients are 𝛄𝛍γ=K−1μ, and their least squares estimates are 𝛄𝛍γ^=K−1μ^;

  3. [1g,C] is nonsingular iff the columns of C are linearly independent and 1g∉C(C);

  4. to make the coefficients estimate prescribed linear functions 𝛍Lμ of the level means, with L a nonsingular g×g matrix, use the coding K=L−1.

prp-est-coding-dual.title: Orthogonal codings
prp-est-coding-dual.html: If the columns of K=[1g,c1,…,cg−1] are mutually orthogonal, then the coefficients of the coded model are 𝛍γ^0=1g∑ky¯k,γ^j=cj⊤μ^cj⊤cj,j=1,…,g−1, whatever the group sizes.

prp-est-contrast-ss.title: Contrasts as projections
prp-est-contrast-ss.html:
Let c and d be contrasts, and write 𝛍ψ^c=c⊤μ^. Then:

  1. ψ^c=uc⊤y, and uc is a nonzero vector in C(Z)∩1⊥;

  2. the sum of squares for the contrast, SS(c)=ψ^c2∑kck2/nk, equals ‖Py‖2, where P is the orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by uc;

  3. Cov(ψ^c,ψ^d)=σ2∑kckdk/nk=σ2uc⊤ud when Cov(Y)=σ2I, so orthogonal contrasts have uncorrelated estimates and orthogonal vectors u;

  4. if c1,…,cg−1 are pairwise orthogonal contrasts, then ∑j=1g−1SS(cj)=∑k=1gnk(y¯k−y¯)2, the sum of squares between levels.

prp-est-coordinate.title: Identifiability of a single coefficient
prp-est-coordinate.html:
Write x1,…,xp for the columns of X. For each j the following are equivalent:

  1. βj is identifiable;

  2. every v∈N(X) has vj=0;

  3. xj is not a linear combination of the other columns of X;

  4. deleting column j from X lowers the rank.

prp-est-identifiable-rank.html: The following are equivalent: (a) 𝛃β is identifiable; (b) N(X)={0}; (c) rank(X)=p; (d) X⊤X is nonsingular. In that case the function h of @thm-est-identifiable-mean for 𝛃𝛃g(β)=β is 𝛍𝛍h(μ)=(X⊤X)−1X⊤μ.

prp-est-interaction.title: Estimability in the interaction model
prp-est-interaction.html:
In the interaction model @eq-est-interaction with m occupied cells, write μij=μ+αi+βj+γij for the mean of an occupied cell.

  1. C(X)=C(\bW) and rank(X)=m: the model is the cell-means model in disguise.

  2. The estimable functions are exactly the linear combinations ∑cijμij over occupied cells.

  3. An interaction contrast ∑i,jdijγij whose coefficient table (dij) has zero row and column sums is estimable iff dij=0 for every empty cell. In particular, γij−γil−γkj+γkl is estimable iff all four cells are occupied.

prp-est-linear-identifiable.html: A linear function 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is identifiable iff 𝛌λ⊥N(X), that is, iff 𝛌λ∈C(X⊤). The identifiable linear functions form a subspace of dimension r=rank(X).

prp-est-ls-estimator.title: Least squares estimation of estimable functions
prp-est-ls-estimator.title_html: Least squares estimation of estimable functions
prp-est-ls-estimator.html:
Let 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β be estimable, with 𝛌𝛒λ=X⊤ρ=X⊤Xr, let 𝛃β^ be any least squares solution and G any generalized inverse of X⊤X. Then:

  1. 𝛌𝛃𝛒𝛌λ⊤β^=ρ⊤My=r⊤X⊤y=λ⊤GX⊤y;

  2. 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃E(λ⊤β^)=λ⊤β;

  3. if Cov(Y)=σ2I, then 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛌𝛌𝛒Var(λ⊤β^)=σ2λ⊤Gλ=σ2r⊤λ=σ2‖Mρ‖2, the same for every G;

  4. more generally, if 𝛃Λ⊤β is estimable, then 𝛃Cov(Λ⊤β^)=σ2Λ⊤GΛ for every G.

prp-est-min-norm-side.title: Minimum norm as a side condition
prp-est-min-norm-side.title_html: Minimum norm as a side condition
prp-est-min-norm-side.html: Let the columns of the p×(p−r) matrix V0 be a basis of N(X). Then T=V0⊤ satisfies the conditions of @thm-est-side-conditions, and the resulting solution 𝛃β^T is the minimum-norm least squares solution X+y.

prp-est-side-meaning.title: Constrained coefficients are estimable functions
prp-est-side-meaning.html: Suppose T satisfies the conditions of @thm-est-side-conditions, and let PT=(X⊤X+T⊤T)−1X⊤X. For each 𝛃β, 𝛃PTβ is the unique vector b with 𝛃Xb=Xβ and Tb=0. The matrix PT is idempotent, with range N(T) and null space N(X). Every row of PT lies in C(X⊤). So each constrained coefficient 𝛃ej⊤PTβ is an estimable function of the original parameters, and 𝛃β^T estimates it without bias.

thm-est-characterization.title: Characterizations of estimability
thm-est-characterization.html:
Let X be n×p, let G denote a generalized inverse of X⊤X, and let 𝛌λ∈Rp. The following are equivalent:

  1. 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable;

  2. 𝛌λ∈C(X⊤): there is 𝛒ρ∈Rn with 𝛌𝛒λ⊤=ρ⊤X;

  3. 𝛌λ⊥N(X): 𝛌λ⊤v=0 whenever Xv=0;

  4. 𝛌λ∈C(X⊤X): the system 𝛌X⊤Xr=λ has a solution;

  5. 𝛌𝛌λ⊤GX⊤X=λ⊤ for some generalized inverse G;

  6. 𝛌𝛌λ⊤GX⊤X=λ⊤ for every generalized inverse G;

  7. for every y, 𝛌λ⊤b has the same value for all solutions b of the normal equations X⊤Xb=X⊤y (@thm-proj-normal-equations);

  8. 𝛌rank(Xλ⊤)=rank(X).

thm-est-connected.title: Connectedness and estimability in the additive model
thm-est-connected.title_html: Connectedness and estimability in the additive model
thm-est-connected.html:
In the additive model @eq-est-additive, let the design graph have c connected components. Then:

  1. rank(X)=a+b−c;

  2. αi−αk is estimable iff levels i and k of A lie in the same component, and likewise for βj−βl;

  3. if the design is connected, the estimable functions are exactly the linear functions of the cell means μ+αi+βj over all cells, occupied or not. In particular every difference between levels of the same factor is estimable.

thm-est-estimable-identifiable.html:
For 𝛌λ∈Rp the following are equivalent:

  1. 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable;

  2. 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is identifiable;

  3. 𝛌λ∈C(X⊤), that is, 𝛌𝛒λ⊤=ρ⊤X for some 𝛒ρ∈Rn.

For a p×q matrix Λ, 𝛃Λ⊤β is estimable iff Λ=X⊤P for some n×q matrix P, that is, iff C(Λ)⊆C(X⊤).

thm-est-identifiable-mean.title: Identifiable means “a function of the mean”
thm-est-identifiable-mean.title_html: Identifiable means “a function of the mean”
thm-est-identifiable-mean.html: A function g on Rp is identifiable iff there is a function h on C(X) with 𝛃𝛃𝛃g(β)=h(Xβ)for every β∈Rp. Equivalently, g is constant on each affine subspace 𝛃β+N(X).

thm-est-oneway-contrasts.title: Estimable functions in the one-way model
thm-est-oneway-contrasts.title_html: Estimable functions in the one-way model
thm-est-oneway-contrasts.html: In the one-way model with every nk≥1, the function λ0μ+∑kλkαk is estimable iff λ0=∑kλk. In particular, a linear function of the effects alone, ∑kckαk, is estimable iff it is a contrast (or zero). For a contrast, the least squares estimator and its variance under Cov(Y)=σ2I are ψ^=∑kcky¯k,Var(ψ^)=σ2∑kck2nk.{#eq-est-contrast-var}

thm-est-reparameterization.title: Reparameterizing to full rank
thm-est-reparameterization.html:
Let rank(X)=r. Let U be an r×p matrix of rank r whose rows lie in C(X⊤), so that 𝛄𝛃γ=Uβ is a vector of r linearly independent estimable functions, and put Z=XU⊤(UU⊤)−1.{#eq-est-reparameterization-matrix}

Then:

  1. X=ZU, Z has full column rank r, and C(Z)=C(X);

  2. the models 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, 𝛃β∈Rp, and 𝛄E(Y)=Zγ, 𝛄γ∈Rr, describe the same set of mean vectors, with 𝛄𝛃γ=Uβ;

  3. the least squares estimate in the new model is 𝛄𝛃γ^=(Z⊤Z)−1Z⊤y=Uβ^ for every least squares solution 𝛃β^ of the old one;

  4. 𝛌𝛃λ⊤β is estimable iff 𝛌λ=U⊤c for some c∈Rr, which is then unique, and in that case 𝛌𝛃𝛄λ⊤β^=c⊤γ^;

  5. conversely, if Z is any n×r matrix of full column rank with C(Z)=C(X), then X=ZU for a unique U, and U has rank r and estimable rows.

thm-est-side-conditions.title: Side conditions
thm-est-side-conditions.html:
Let X be n×p of rank r and T be q×p. The following are equivalent:

  1. for every y∈Rn there is exactly one b with X⊤Xb=X⊤y and Tb=0;

  2. for every 𝛍μ∈C(X) there is exactly one b with 𝛍Xb=μ and Tb=0;

  3. Rp=N(X)⊕N(T);

  4. rank(XT)=p and C(T⊤)∩C(X⊤)={0};

  5. rank(T)=p−r, and no nonzero linear combination of the rows of T is estimable.

When these hold, X⊤X+T⊤T is nonsingular, the solution in (a) is 𝛃β^T=(X⊤X+T⊤T)−1X⊤y,{#eq-est-side-solution}

and (X⊤X+T⊤T)−1 is a generalized inverse of X⊤X.
